insight: Einarsson v. Canada (ICSID UNCT/20/6) is the first publicly documented ISDS case resting centrally on proprietary data (marine seismic survey data) asserted as a trade-secret and copyright-protected investment under NAFTA Chapter 11; challenged measure is Canada's regulatory disclosure regime (Canada Petroleum Resources Act); jurisdictional objection is the NAFTA Article 1121 waiver requirement. Merits hearing concluded March 2025; award pending. Structurally analogous to the three-ring pattern but in the oil-and-gas sector, not pharma.

The USMCA effectively eliminated ISDS between Canada and the United States; the three-year legacy period expired 30 June 2023, foreclosing any successor to Eli Lilly v. Canada under the principal North American framework. No pharmaceutical IP ISDS claim against Canada can now be filed by a US investor under any USMCA provision.

No publicly known ISDS case has been filed or decided with pharmaceutical trade secrets or clinical trial data as the primary covered investment. The Ferguson/Kim framework remains theoretical and unlitigated. Einarsson (non-pharma data) is the nearest structural analogue.

China's NMPA Implementation Measures for Drug Trial Data Protection (effective May 2026) create formal, protectable, and tradable entitlements in pharmaceutical clinical trial data and marketing authorisation certificates — establishing the Ring 1 foundation for potential future ISDS claims under China's BIT network if protections are subsequently restricted or unevenly applied.

Jason Yu Song v. China (PCA 2019-39, Final Award January 2025) reveals a structural gap in Denial of Benefits clause architecture: existing DOB clauses address corporate third-country nationality but not natural persons who acquire citizenship to access treaty protection. China's nationality-planning argument failed on admissibility (time-bar); the doctrinal gap remains unaddressed.

The CPTPP also forecloses a direct ISDS pathway for pharmaceutical clinical data exclusivity claims: the TPP's data exclusivity obligations for pharmaceutical undisclosed test data (Art. 18.50 of the original TPP) were suspended when the US withdrew, and Chapter 18 IP obligations cannot be directly enforced via ISDS in any event (only Chapter 9 Section A investment standards can). No pharmaceutical IP ISDS case has been filed under CPTPP. UK accession (December 2024) adds investor pool but does not restore suspended provisions. Combined with the USMCA closure, both principal multilateral frameworks available to pharmaceutical investors now lack a direct clinical-data ISDS hook.

The China-Switzerland BIT (2009) explicitly includes 'know-how' in its investment definition (alongside copyrights, patents, and trade marks), making it the most legally specific existing treaty vehicle for asserting pharmaceutical clinical trial data as a covered investment against China. 'Know-how' is the natural treaty characterisation of confidential proprietary research data and does not depend on domestic trade-secret or copyright law. Combined with China's NMPA 2026 pharmaceutical data exclusivity framework, this BIT provides the most credible existing three-ring pathway for the Ferguson/Kim clinical data scenario, with Swiss pharmaceutical investors (Roche, Novartis, Lonza) as the most plausible future claimants.

NAFTA Article 1121's waiver-consistency requirement constitutes a second, independent Ring 3 jurisdictional mechanism in data-as-investment cases, distinct from the Philip Morris abuse-of-rights pattern. The claimant must not only file a written waiver of parallel proceedings but must act consistently with it. Failure to do so — i.e., continuing to pursue damages claims in domestic forums after submission — deprives the tribunal of jurisdiction (Waste Management I, Detroit International Bridge). Canada's Art. 1121 objection in Einarsson v. Canada (UNCT/20/6) invokes exactly this: if sustained, the tribunal is dismissed without reaching the data-as-investment question. This mechanism turns on the claimant's post-waiver litigation conduct, not on corporate restructuring or treaty-shopping.

UNCITRAL WG III denial-of-benefits reform is converging on a July 2026 Commission deliverable focused on procedural elements (Draft Provision 9 in WP.253, renumbered from Draft Provision 17). The 9th intersessional (November 2025, Santiago) and 53rd session (January 2026, New York) confirm the trajectory: 'feasible over transformative.' The natural-person nationality-planning gap revealed by Jason Yu Song v. China is not confirmed as addressed by any draft provision and is very unlikely to be included in the July 2026 package. Ring 3 doctrine architecture unchanged pending July 2026 Commission outcome.

The China-Germany BIT (2003) explicitly includes 'trade and business secrets' in its Article 1 investment definition — alongside 'know-how,' 'technical processes,' and other IP categories — making it the most legally direct existing treaty-text vehicle for asserting pharmaceutical trade secrets as a covered investment against China. This goes beyond the China-Switzerland BIT (2009) ('know-how' only) and matches the Ferguson/Kim framework's core concept most precisely. The China-France BIT (2007) also covers 'know-how.' Combined, all three major European pharmaceutical investor home states (Germany: Bayer, Merck KGaA; Switzerland: Roche, Novartis; France: Sanofi) now have documented treaty-text Ring 1 bases under their China BITs. European BIT architecture survey complete.

The UNCITRAL 59th Commission session (June 29–July 10, 2026, New York) opens in three days — the milestone T05 has been tracking. The Commission deliverable is A/CN.9/1246 ('Draft supplementary provisions on the conduct of proceedings'), a procedural Protocol only: evidence, bifurcation, interim measures, manifest lack of legal merit, security for costs, TPF disclosure, counterclaims, cost allocation. The denial-of-benefits provision (Draft Provision 9, WP.253) is NOT in A/CN.9/1246. The natural-person nationality-planning gap from Jason Yu Song v. China (PCA 2019-39) is not addressed by the July 2026 Commission package. Ring 3 doctrine architecture is unchanged pending the session outcome (expected by July 10, 2026).

The 2026 USTR Special 301 Report (May 2026) formally characterises China's pharmaceutical trial data protection conditions as imposing 'unfair and discriminatory conditions on the effective protection against unfair commercial use, as well as unauthorized disclosure, of undisclosed test or other data generated to obtain marketing approval for pharmaceutical products.' The specific discriminatory gap: China's final measures do not address the protection period for drugs first approved outside China — disadvantaging exactly the European multinational originators (Bayer, Merck KGaA, Roche, Novartis, Sanofi) who are the most plausible Ring 1 BIT claimants. The US has no BIT with China and cannot pursue ISDS; European BIT holders can, and could reference the USTR characterisation to corroborate a Ring 2 discriminatory treatment argument under the China-Germany (2003), China-Switzerland (2009), or China-France (2007) BITs. This is the first identified government-level characterisation of China's pharmaceutical data conditions as potentially discriminatory — converging the Ring 1 foundation (NMPA 2026 measures creating the investment) with the Ring 2 trigger (discriminatory application). Additionally, the June 5, 2026 transitional deadline has passed: companies that failed to submit data protection requests to China's CDE by that date have definitively waived pharmaceutical data exclusivity rights, crystallising which investors hold formal entitlements that could found a BIT claim.

Hela Schwarz GmbH v. People's Republic of China (ICSID ARB/17/19), final award December 10, 2025, is the first decided ICSID case under the China-Germany BIT (2003) — the treaty identified as the primary Ring 1 vehicle for pharmaceutical trade secrets. The tribunal dismissed all EUR 90+ million claims on both jurisdiction and merits grounds. The jurisdictional ground is the BIT's concurrent-proceedings / court-withdrawal requirement: because the claimant's Chinese subsidiary had filed the same claim before Chinese domestic courts before the ICSID arbitration was commenced, the tribunal held the arbitration invalid. This constitutes a third Ring 3 mechanism for the China pharmaceutical data ISDS scenario, distinct from the Philip Morris critical-date / abuse-of-rights doctrine and the NAFTA Art. 1121 waiver mechanism. A European pharmaceutical investor seeking to challenge a Chinese NMPA pharmaceutical data exclusivity decision under the China-Germany BIT (2003) must first withdraw any concurrent Chinese administrative appeals or court proceedings before filing at ICSID — a step that conflicts with the investor's natural first resort to domestic remedies. Counsel for China: A&O Shearman + Ministry of Commerce. Presiding Arbitrator: Sir Daniel Bethlehem KC. Specific BIT article unconfirmed (PDF blocked); holding confirmed from CDR News, A&O Shearman, italaw, and UNCTAD Navigator at high confidence.

The Swedish Supreme Court ruled on June 26, 2026 (reversing the Svea Court of Appeal's November 12, 2024 annulment) that an MFN clause in a bilateral investment treaty can confer tribunal competence by importing a more favourable dispute resolution provision from another BIT. Procedural chain: (1) SCC Partial Final Award on Jurisdiction (August 31, 2022) — MFN allowed, SCC jurisdiction upheld by tribunal; (2) Svea Court of Appeal (November 12, 2024) — MFN cannot import forum from another treaty, award annulled; (3) Swedish Supreme Court (leave granted September 22, 2025; ruling June 26, 2026) — reversed, MFN CAN confer forum competence. The underlying dispute (Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia, SCC Case No. V 2019/058) is a Georgian tax/expropriation claim by a dual Georgian-British national — no IP content. Ring 3 significance: confirms that dual-national investors excluded from ICSID may use MFN clauses to access alternative forums (SCC arbitration under a third BIT) in SCC-seated, Swedish-law arbitrations — a marginal expansion of the Ring 3 jurisdictional toolkit. Full ruling text (NJA citation) not accessible; existence and holding confirmed at medium-high confidence from Swedish Supreme Court news service (search-engine-recovered snippet, June 26, 2026) and IAReporter headline (June 29, 2026).

Three pre-session sources not previously in the project record — EJIL:Talk 'UNCITRAL and ISDS Reform: Moving to the Delivery Phase' (June 2026), ICLRC.ru 'draft provisions on ISDS-specific arbitration procedures almost finalised,' and Kluwer Arbitration Blog's Inaugural Washington Arbitration Week post (May/June 2026) — converge on a more definitive characterisation of the 59th Commission session (opened June 29, 2026): the UNCITRAL reform process has entered its 'delivery phase' and the Procedural Protocol (A/CN.9/1246) is expected to be adopted, not merely considered. The code of conduct for arbitrators and Advisory Centre statute were already adopted in prior sessions; the Protocol completes the programme. For Ring 3: even adoption of the Protocol would not address the denial-of-benefits provision (Draft Provision 9) or the natural-person nationality-planning gap (Jason Yu Song scenario). Those structural gaps in Ring 3 doctrine persist regardless of the session outcome. Day 1 proceedings coverage not available (session opened 10:30 a.m. June 29; real-time indexing lag expected).

Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia (SCC Case No. V2019/058): the Swedish Supreme Court (June 15, 2026) reversed the Svea Court of Appeal (November 12, 2024) and held that the MFN clause in Article 3(3) of the Georgia-UK BIT (1995) — which explicitly extends MFN treatment to all provisions in Articles 1–11, including Article 8 on dispute settlement — allows a dual Georgian-British investor to import multi-forum arbitral access (including SCC) from the Georgia-BLEU BIT, thereby establishing SCC jurisdiction over a case where the home BIT designated ICSID as the exclusive forum (unavailable to the investor as a Georgian national). This is the first Swedish Supreme Court ruling establishing MFN-forum-access in investment arbitration as a jurisdictional mechanism for dual nationals. No IP nexus (tobacco sector, tax enforcement measure); Ring 3 near-miss — enriches the background MFN + dual-nationality jurisdictional admissibility landscape without advancing the pharmaceutical trade secret or clinical data thread specifically. Outcome confirmed; full judgment text paywalled (IAReporter).

A/CN.9/1246 (UNCITRAL, April 15, 2026 advance copy) does not finalize the temporal scope of its supplementary provisions but uses April 1, 2027 as an illustrative example ('they could apply, for example, to treaties concluded on or after 1 April 2027, if [certain conditions relating to] UARs are met') while noting the scope-of-application provision 'may need to be developed.' The Protocol's non-retroactivity was therefore not a finalized provision in the draft submitted to the Commission; the temporal scope was a live question at the 59th Commission session (June 29–July 10, 2026). Additionally, A/CN.9/1246 explicitly proposes a Mauritius Convention-type opt-in mechanism to make the Protocol applicable to pre-existing investment treaties — meaning the China-Germany BIT (2003), China-Switzerland BIT (2009), and China-France BIT (2007) are not definitively excluded from Protocol coverage if the relevant parties opt in via a future Mauritius-type convention. This corrects the prior framing (which treated the April 1, 2027 date as a confirmed cutoff) and adds the Mauritius opt-in dimension as a live architectural possibility documented within the draft.

Confirmed from practitioner and academic secondary sources (MEDIUM confidence) that Chinese BITs explicitly exclude MFN extension to procedural ISDS rights — the Okuashvili MFN-forum-bypass mechanism (Swedish SC, June 2026) is architecturally closed for European pharmaceutical investors under the China-Germany BIT (2003), China-Switzerland BIT (2009), and China-France BIT (2007). Four-mechanism Ring 3 taxonomy now complete: (1) Philip Morris abuse-of-rights/critical-date [applicable to China BIT scenario]; (2) NAFTA Art. 1121 waiver-consistency [NAFTA/CUSMA-specific; inapplicable to China BITs]; (3) Hela Schwarz concurrent-proceedings/court-withdrawal [directly applicable — China-Germany BIT]; (4) Okuashvili MFN-scope bypass [CLOSED — Chinese BITs exclude MFN from ISDS]. For China pharmaceutical BIT scenario: only mechanisms 1 and 3 are operative Ring 3 gates.

China SAMR Order No. 126 (Provisions on the Protection of Trade Secrets, issued February 24, 2026, effective June 1, 2026) — the most substantial overhaul of China's administrative trade secret enforcement framework in approximately 30 years — explicitly includes 'data, algorithms, and computer program code' as categories of technical information eligible for trade secret protection. Article 29 establishes extraterritorial reach. Administrative enforcement: injunctions and fines up to 5M RMB (no damages). Pharmaceutical clinical trial data falls within the broadened 'data' category by inclusion; the Provisions do not specifically address pharmaceutical or clinical data. This creates a parallel administrative enforcement channel for pharmaceutical trade secrets running alongside the NMPA Implementation Measures for Drug Trial Data Protection (effective May 15, 2026). For the China-Germany BIT (2003)'s 'trade and business secrets' investment-definition language, China's own administrative law now formally characterizes data as a protectable trade secret. [Analytical inference: no practitioner source connects SAMR Order No. 126 to ISDS or BIT investment definitions; regulatory facts confirmed from multiple secondary sources at medium-high confidence; Provisions text not directly read.]

Wingtech Technology (China) / Yuching Holding Limited (HK) issued a formal notice of dispute under the China-Netherlands BIT (Article 10(3)) on October 15, 2025, seeking USD ~8 billion in damages over the Dutch government's emergency order (Goods Availability Act, September 2025) preventing transfer of 'intellectual property rights' and production assets to China. This is the first confirmed Ring 1–2 near-miss under the China–European BIT network since the project began monitoring: IP/technology assets are the central protected investment; the governmental measure directly targets IP transfer. The China-Netherlands BIT contains no national security carve-out — architecturally parallel to the China-Germany BIT (2003) that governs the pharmaceutical trade-secret scenario in reverse. The six-month cooling-off period expired ~April 15, 2026; ICSID formal filing is unconfirmed. The claimant's 'multi-track legal strategy' (parallel Enterprise Chamber domestic proceedings + BIT notice) mirrors the concurrent-proceedings structure that caused Hela Schwarz v. China to fail on jurisdiction. [Inverse scenario: Chinese investor, European respondent — near-miss, not pharmaceutical. Facts at medium-high confidence from Kluwer, AMS Advocaten, NL Times, CELIS. BIT/Ring relevance is a research inference at medium confidence.]

The Statute of the Advisory Centre on International Investment Dispute Resolution was adopted 'in principle' at the 57th UNCITRAL Commission Session in 2024 — not first adopted at the 59th session (July 2026). The 16-article statute was finalized in 2024; the 59th session concerns operationalization (host country, budget, governance) and preparing the statute for formal UN General Assembly adoption in December 2026. This completes and corrects the three-deliverable reform sequence: (1) Code of Conduct for Arbitrators — 56th session (July 2023, UNGA Res. 78/105); (2) Advisory Centre Statute in principle — 57th session (2024); (3) Procedural Protocol (A/CN.9/1246) — expected 59th session (July 2026). The ISDS reform architecture is further along than the prior record indicated on this point. [Not a Ring 1/2/3 pharmaceutical IP finding; corrects UNCITRAL reform timeline in background architecture context. STATE_OF_THE_ANSWER framing updated.]

Jason Yu Song v. People's Republic of China (PCA 2019-39, China-UK BIT 1986) — the only publicly known ISDS award against China [unverified: claim from CMS-lawnow search summary; may carry qualifications] — survived two Swiss Federal Supreme Court set-aside applications: (1) First challenge (4A_46/2024) dismissed April 17, 2025; (2) Second challenge (4A_528/2024) dismissed June 26, 2025 (published July 21, 2025). The second challenge invoked a Chinese criminal court judgment issued during the arbitration as new evidence that the investment was made illegally, arguing this retroactively deprived the tribunal of jurisdiction. The Swiss FSC rejected both challenges; the award (USD 26,045,613.90 + interest) is definitively final. This documents China's post-award resistance arsenal: (a) standard set-aside application; (b) criminal-conviction-as-illegality-of-investment post-award jurisdictional attack, rejected in Swiss-seated proceedings. No IP nexus (land-rights expropriation, Shanxi Province). Ring 3 relevance: the full challenge sequence a pharmaceutical investor would face in a China BIT claim extends beyond the three pre-ICSID-filing Ring 3 gates (Philip Morris abuse-of-rights; Hela Schwarz fork-in-the-road; MFN-closed) to include this post-award resistance layer. Both known mechanisms — standard set-aside and criminal-conviction illegality attack — have been judicially rejected in the sole decided case.

Wingtech/Nexperia concurrent-proceedings architecture updated (July 2026): the project's July 5 record of 'multi-track strategy (Enterprise Chamber + BIT notice)' was incomplete. Wingtech has since filed (a) an Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law (AFSL) claim in China's Dongguan Intermediate People's Court, accepted May 22, 2026, against Nexperia Holding B.V., Nexperia B.V., ITEC B.V., and three named individuals (CEO Tilger, COO Kempe, CLO Lichtenberg), seeking CNY 8B (~EUR 1B) in damages; and (b) a new Dutch court proceeding against Nexperia's Dutch entities (June 8, 2026; specifics body-blocked). Multi-track now covers at least 4 concurrent proceedings alongside the China-Netherlands BIT notice. Critically, the China-Netherlands BIT (2001) Article 10 has an asymmetric concurrent-proceedings architecture: for investments in the Netherlands (Wingtech's situation), the investor may submit to international arbitration 'at any time' — no withdrawal requirement. For investments in China, a withdrawal-before-judgment requirement applies. The Chinese AFSL claim (against Nexperia entities and individuals; AFSL legal basis; Dongguan court) is different in parties, legal basis, and forum from the BIT claim (against Netherlands state; BIT basis; ICSID) — the 'triple identity test' would likely not be met, so the AFSL claim does not trigger a concurrent-proceedings bar to BIT arbitration. ICSID registration still unconfirmed as of Day 85 post-cooling-off. [MEDIUM-HIGH confidence for AFSL facts: Bloomberg, Caixin, SCMP, Global Times. MEDIUM confidence for BIT Article 10 architecture: secondary-source search summaries; primary Article 10 text not directly read. Inverse scenario — Chinese investor, European respondent; near-miss, not pharmaceutical.]
confidence: medium-high for AFSL facts; medium for BIT Article 10 architecture

insight: Article 9(c) of the Protocol to the China-Germany BIT (2003) — the concurrent-proceedings provision applied in Hela Schwarz GmbH v. People's Republic of China (ICSID ARB/17/19, Award December 10, 2025) — has been reconstructed from a search-engine snippet of the JIDS 2020 academic article ('Parallel Proceedings under Chinese BITs: The Case of Hela Schwarz GmbH v PR China,' JIDS vol. 11(2): 335). Provision text: 'in case the issue has been brought to a Chinese court, it can be withdrawn by the investor according to Chinese law.' Confirms: (1) Article 9(c) sub-provision upgraded from LOWER to MEDIUM-HIGH confidence; (2) no-U-turn label confirmed from provision text — withdrawal is the prescribed cure mechanism; (3) cure pathway requires withdrawal 'according to Chinese law'; (4) Hela Schwarz claimant argued the provision was 'irrelevant, given that no domestic proceedings were pending at the time it filed the request for arbitration' — but tribunal dismissed on jurisdiction regardless, suggesting the 'has been brought' language may capture completed, not only pending, proceedings. Primary BIT text and Award PDF remain 403-blocked; provision text is from a secondary academic source (JIDS) via search-engine snippet.

Okuashvili v. Georgia (SCC Case V2019/058) — posture correction and new detail (MEDIUM-HIGH confidence). The Swedish Supreme Court (June 26, 2026) did not directly restore the SCC arbitration after reversing the Svea Court of Appeal's November 12, 2024 annulment. Instead, it remanded the case to the Svea Court of Appeal to address 'legal points left unresolved in the lower instance proceedings.' The project record's prior framing — 'confirmed posture: jurisdiction restored by Supreme Court; case proceeds on merits at SCC' — is inaccurate. The correct posture is: MFN-forum-access holding established (unanimously) by the SC; case remanded to Svea CoA for further annulment proceedings; SCC arbitration remains suspended pending Svea CoA completion. The 'legal points left unresolved' likely include annulment grounds other than the MFN-scope question (which the SC resolved) that the Svea CoA had not reached in November 2024 because it disposed of the annulment on the MFN-scope ground alone. This answers the open thread question ('is SCC jurisdiction fully restored or subject to a remaining Svea remand?'): remand confirmed, SCC not yet restored. The decision is also characterized as unanimous. Source: Westerberg & Partners, 'Hallmark victory before the Swedish Supreme Court' (winning party's counsel; body 403-blocked; text from search-engine snippets consistent across two independent queries). No IP nexus — tobacco sector, tax enforcement. Ring 3 significance: the MFN-forum-access doctrine is now confirmed at Swedish Supreme Court level, but its practical application in this case remains suspended pending Svea CoA remand proceedings. The China BIT MFN architectural closure (July 2 finding) is unaffected.

Protocol Article 9(a) of the China-Germany BIT (2003) imposes a mandatory administrative-exhaustion pre-condition to ICSID arbitration — a German investor 'may submit a dispute for arbitration only if the investor has referred the issue to an administrative review procedure according to Chinese law.' This is a distinct and earlier pre-ICSID gate from the concurrent-proceedings/court-withdrawal bar in Article 9(c). China raised Article 9(a) in Hela Schwarz GmbH v. People's Republic of China (ICSID ARB/17/19) as a 'compulsory precondition qualifying the Respondent's offer to arbitrate'; the Claimant did not allege compliance in its Memorial. The Award (December 10, 2025) addressed China's 'third objection' based on Article 9(a). The tribunal's specific disposition on Article 9(a) — whether sustained or rejected — is UNCONFIRMED (Award PDF 403-blocked; A&O Shearman and CDR News framing emphasized the Art. 9(c) 'court withdrawal' issue). For the pharmaceutical China-Germany BIT scenario: the two Protocol Article 9 gates are structurally sequential and in tension — Art. 9(a) requires exhaustion of Chinese administrative review (the natural first regulatory challenge step), while Art. 9(c) bars ICSID filing if the investor has also filed in Chinese courts. Pursuing administrative review (9(a)) and then court review creates the exact domestic footprint that 9(c) may subsequently bar. Together they form a two-track pre-ICSID architecture that is more complex than the project record had previously mapped. [MEDIUM confidence for provision content — reconstructed from respondent's argument in JIDS 2020 secondary source; verbatim Article 9(a) text not recovered; tribunal disposition UNCONFIRMED.]

The UNCITRAL 59th Commission session (June 29–July 10, 2026, New York) adopted two named instruments: (1) 'Supplementary Provisions on the Conduct of Proceedings' (based on A/CN.9/1246, covering TPF disclosure, cost allocation, early dismissal, bifurcation, security for costs, counterclaims, interim measures) and (2) the 'Statute of the Advisory Centre on International Investment Dispute Resolution.' Neither instrument includes the Denial of Benefits provision (Draft Provision 9 / WP.253) or addresses the natural-person nationality planning gap identified in Jason Yu Song v. China. The MIIR (Multilateral Instrument to Implement Reforms), which would enable opt-in coverage of pre-existing bilateral investment treaties, was not adopted at this session and remains a future milestone. For Ring 3 pharmaceutical trade-secret China BIT claims: the adopted Supplementary Provisions do not alter the pre-ICSID gate architecture (Protocol Ad Article 9(a) administrative exhaustion; Ad Article 9(c) concurrent-proceedings bar under China-Germany BIT 2003; Philip Morris abuse-of-rights). Ring 3 doctrine architecture for pharmaceutical China BIT claims is unchanged by the July 2026 ISDS reform adoption. [MEDIUM confidence: adoption characterization from post-session civil-society analysis by Fernando Hernandez Espino / Both ENDS / AFTINET, July 2026, body 403-blocked; IISD ITN/EJIL:Talk post-session coverage not yet indexed.]

Protocol Ad Article 9(b) of the China-Germany BIT (2003) imposes a mandatory three-month temporal gate between initiation of Chinese administrative review (Ad Article 9(a)) and ICSID arbitration filing: 'the dispute still exists three months after he has brought the issue to the review procedure.' This condition was not previously documented in the project record, completing the three-condition pre-ICSID architecture for the first time: (a) mandatory administrative review referral; (b) three-month waiting period; (c) withdrawal of any concurrent Chinese court proceedings. For a pharmaceutical investor challenging an NMPA data exclusivity decision under the China-Germany BIT (2003), the pre-ICSID path requires: file administrative appeal → wait three months → withdraw any concurrent Chinese court proceedings → only then file at ICSID. The temporal gate (9(b)) means administrative exhaustion (9(a)) alone is insufficient; a minimum elapsed-time condition must also be satisfied. Together, the three conditions form a sequential process that is more complex and time-consuming than the project record had previously mapped. Text recovered from search-engine snippet reconstructing the Protocol Article 9 text; consistent with previously confirmed 9(a) (JIDS 2020, July 15) and 9(c) (JIDS 2020, July 11); primary PDF not directly read.

AsiaPhos Limited and Norwest Chemicals Pte Ltd v. People's Republic of China (ICSID ADM/21/1, Award February 16, 2023) is the second publicly decided ICSID case in which China obtained a jurisdictional dismissal under a Chinese BIT, and the first under the 1985 China-Singapore BIT. The tribunal found ISDS jurisdiction limited to 'disputes regarding the amount of compensation for expropriation' under Article 13(3) of the China-Singapore BIT (1985) — a first-generation scope limitation — and declined jurisdiction over all substantive claims (expropriation occurrence, FET, FPS). China's restrictive jurisdictional rationale was affirmed by the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (4A_172/2023, January 11, 2024). An ICSID Review case note (vol. 39, no. 1, p. 29, 2024) exists; publication ~20 months post-award, suggesting the Hela Schwarz case note is not expected until August–October 2027. This identifies a fifth Ring 3 mechanism in the China BIT landscape: first-generation BIT ISDS scope limitation (expropriation-compensation-quantum only). This mechanism is inapplicable to the European pharmaceutical trade-secret scenario under the third-generation China-Germany BIT (2003), which provides full ISDS access. The case enriches the project record as background evidence of China's consistent jurisdictional-gatekeeping posture and prompts the Ring 3 taxonomy update from four to five mechanisms. Mining sector (phosphate); no IP nexus. MEDIUM-HIGH confidence: case existence, award date, Swiss FSC affirmance, and ICSID Review case note confirmed from multiple independent sources; full Award text and ICSID Review article body not directly read (403-blocked).

The China-Netherlands BIT (2001) Exchange of Notes/Protocol contains a mandatory administrative review exhaustion pre-condition for investments in China: 'The Kingdom of the Netherlands took note that the People's Republic of China requires investors to exhaust the domestic administrative review procedure specified by Chinese laws and regulations before submission of a dispute to international arbitration under Article 10, paragraph 3, with such procedure taking a maximum period of three months.' This parallels the China-Germany BIT (2003) Protocol Article 9(a) administrative exhaustion requirement and Article 9(b) three-month temporal gate, confirming that China's pre-ICSID administrative review exhaustion architecture is a cross-BIT structural feature, not unique to one treaty. As of the July 9, 2026 project record, the China-Netherlands BIT entry documented the court-withdrawal asymmetric architecture (Article 10); today's finding adds the administrative exhaustion pre-condition as a separately documented layer. For Wingtech/Nexperia's claim (Netherlands as respondent, Dutch investment), this provision is inapplicable given Article 10's asymmetric structure (no concurrent-proceedings bar for Netherlands-side investments). For a hypothetical European pharmaceutical investor challenging a Chinese regulatory decision under the China-Netherlands BIT, the same two-step domestic engagement + court withdrawal architecture as the China-Germany BIT applies. Source: search-engine result summary of China-Netherlands BIT Exchange of Notes text (ASEAN Briefing PDF, 403-blocked for direct fetch); consistent with UNCTAD Navigator and Netherlands ILR (Springer). MEDIUM confidence: provision text characterization from indirect source; primary Exchange of Notes text not directly read.

Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. v. Kingdom of Sweden (ICSID ARB/22/2) — post-hearing Chinese investor claim against European respondent state, the most advanced pending ICSID case involving a Chinese investor and a European state under a China-European BIT involving technology assets. Merits hearing: November 25–December 5, 2024 (Stockholm); award pending. Treaty basis: China-Sweden BIT (1982) + Protocol (2004). The claim follows Sweden's decision to exclude Huawei and ZTE from 5G infrastructure procurement on national security grounds. The European Commission appeared as non-disputing party (NDP) — the first known EC NDP appearance in a Chinese-investor BIT case against a European state, reflecting EU-level institutional engagement with Chinese-investor BIT claims. Technology assets (5G telecommunications equipment, infrastructure contracts) asserted as covered investments. National security defense raised and heard on the merits. Architectural significance: (1) First publicly known ICSID arbitration to proceed to a merits hearing under the China-Sweden BIT; (2) the award will be the first ICSID decision on whether a European state's national-security-motivated exclusion of a Chinese technology company from public procurement constitutes a BIT violation; (3) European Commission NDP appearance sets precedent for EU institutional engagement with Chinese-investor BIT claims; (4) technology assets plus national security defense on merits creates a direct structural parallel to the pharmaceutical trade-secret scenario. This is the inverse scenario of the pharmaceutical research question (Chinese investor, European respondent; technology assets, not clinical data), but architecturally the closest active ICSID analogue. Cited in Gáspár-Szilágyi, 'When the Dragon Comes Home to Roost: Chinese Outbound Investment Arbitration Claims and the Boundaries of the BIT' (JIDS 2024) as a leading example; open-access Cardiff PDF confirmed for the article. China-Sweden BIT (1982/2004) Protocol administrative exhaustion characterization: appears to use permissive 'may require' language (structural parallel to China-Switzerland BIT (2009) Protocol) — UNCONFIRMED; China-Sweden BIT Protocol text not directly read. HIGH confidence for case existence, merits hearing completion, and European Commission NDP; MEDIUM confidence for Protocol administrative exhaustion characterization.

China-Switzerland BIT (2009) Protocol uses permissive 'may require' administrative exhaustion language — structurally distinct from the mandatory pre-ICSID administrative review required by the China-Germany BIT (2003) Protocol Article 9(a) and China-Netherlands BIT (2001) Exchange of Notes. The China-Switzerland BIT Protocol provides (reconstructed from search-engine summaries; primary Protocol text 403-blocked): 'the competent authorities of the People's Republic of China may require an investor ... to exhaust domestic administrative review procedures specified under Chinese laws and regulations before submission of a dispute to international arbitration under Article 9.' The permissive 'may require' formulation makes the administrative exhaustion pre-condition discretionary — China must affirmatively invoke it; it is not self-executing on the investor. By contrast, the China-Germany BIT (2003) Protocol Article 9(a) uses mandatory language ('may submit ... only if the investor has referred the issue to an administrative review procedure according to Chinese law') and the China-Netherlands BIT (2001) Exchange of Notes uses similar mandatory framing ('requires investors to exhaust the domestic administrative review procedure'). The China-Sweden BIT (1982/2004) Protocol appears to use the same permissive 'may require' structure — UNCONFIRMED for China-Sweden specifically (structural inference). If China does not invoke its discretionary exhaustion right, a Swiss pharmaceutical investor (Roche, Novartis, Lonza) could file directly at ICSID after the standard cooling-off period, bypassing the mandatory administrative-exhaustion first step required of China-Germany BIT investors. Combined with the China-Switzerland BIT's explicit 'know-how' Ring 1 coverage, the China-Switzerland BIT currently offers the best combined Ring 1 plus Ring 3 profile among the European China BITs in scope for a pharmaceutical trade-secret ISDS claim against China. insight: Fetch-relay semantics established from source (scripts/fetch_relay.py), correcting the record: 'find' is matched case-insensitively (body.lower().find(find.lower())) against text with ALL HTML tags stripped including their attributes, so a string present only inside an href is invisible to the relay — which makes a relay null about RENDERED TEXT, weaker in mechanism than a raw-HTML null. find_matched is `bool(find) and bool(excerpt)`, NOT bool(excerpt) alone (fetch_relay.py:181-182); the omitted conjunct is why an empty-find control row correctly reads find_matched false despite a non-empty excerpt. excerpt_of sets start = idx - EXCERPT_CHARS//4, so every matching row gets the same 100 characters of left context and up to 300 of right — the window is not 'centred' and no row has a 'wider' left window than another. The productive query form is to anchor on a neighbouring structural label and read the value out of the window; two anchors chosen on opposite sides of a target bracket a cell value and prove the page's element ordering at the same time. Separately: equal byte length across fetches with differing sha256 is MOST CONSISTENT WITH an origin-side constant-width varying field (a nonce) rather than a content change, but it is not proof and it is not load-bearing — confirmation should rest on identity of the retrieved excerpt text, and near-simultaneous same-run fetches are one time point, not several observations.

The fetch relay's `find` selects a POSITION, not a PROPOSITION — request-echo and boilerplate-preemption are one defect with two faces, both yielding an uninformative find_matched: true. `excerpt_of` (scripts/fetch_relay.py:130-135) returns the window around the FIRST case-insensitive match via str.find, with start = idx - EXCERPT_CHARS//4 = idx - 100. Proved by arithmetic on the 2026-08-05 `Mapped by` row: the excerpt's match sits at offset exactly 100, inside the IIA Mapping Project's disclaimer prose ('Individual treaties are mapped by law students...'), so the per-treaty attribution label was never asked for. CONSEQUENT CLASSIFICATION RULE: such a row is MIS-ANCHORED, not null — a null says the page was asked and did not answer; a mis-anchored row says the question was never put, and recording the second as the first enters a false negative about a live source. OPERATIVE DISCIPLINE: before firing a row, answer 'is the first occurrence of this string in the tag-stripped body the occurrence I want?'; where the honest answer is 'I cannot know', write the row up as a PROBE with what a miss would mean stated in advance. Corollary: the reduction reports no offset, so a mis-anchored row cannot diagnose itself; adding match_offset and body_chars would make it self-diagnosing (PROPOSED ONLY, not built).

The fetch relay is structurally incapable of DELIVERING A DOCUMENT, by design rather than defect, in three independent ways: (1) it cannot report a URL that appears ONLY inside an attribute, because _ANY_TAG_RE = re.compile(r'<[^>]+>') (:79) strips every tag including attributes before any matching (:126-128) — a URL printed as visible body text DOES survive, and final_url is reported, so the limitation is attribute-scoped, not absolute; (2) it returns no text at all for a PDF, because excerpt_of gates on content-type (:124-125), so excerpt is '' and find_matched is false BY CONSTRUCTION — DEMONSTRATED, not merely derived, at analytics/fetch-results/2026-08-03-control.json record 1 (sps.pdf, HTTP 200, 2,104,033 bytes, excerpt ''); (3) EXCERPT_CHARS=400 with a literal-only find and MAX_URLS=12 makes a chained provision-read circular — you must already know a string is in the document to anchor on it. PRE-EMPTIVE BINDING RULE: a PDF row's find_matched: false is guaranteed by the content-type gate and is NEVER evidence of textual absence. Consequence for research routing: an unread treaty instrument is not relay-work and no relay budget should be spent on it; the relay can only ever provide a provenance fixture (existence + byte length + sha256 at a named locator), never a reading.

THE COUNCIL'S OUTPUT WAS NOT REACHING ITS READER, and the failure is silent at both ends. `.github/workflows/daily-update.yml` triggers `on: push` under analytics/daily-research/** with NO `branches:` filter, and scripts/send_daily_update.py de-duplicates to one email per day via a DATE-ADDRESSED marker at analytics/daily-research/.sent/<DATE>. When the council switched from a single [skip ci] commit to named incremental part-commits on 2026-07-31, the FIRST push began winning the email and every later part was de-duplicated away — silently falsifying the workflow's own header comment, which asserts it does not rely on the push trigger. MEASURED day by day from runner logs at each sending run's head_sha: over seven council days a COMPLETE record reached the operator TWICE (2026-07-31, 2026-08-02), both by accident of commit timing. 2026-08-03 truncated after Part 3 (41% missing, entire close-out); 2026-08-04 truncated after Part 1 (93% missing — analyst memo, eight sustained objections, close-out); 2026-08-05 truncated after Part 1; 2026-07-30 and 2026-08-01 NEVER DELIVERED, each with an end-of-day ALERT declaring no record existed, and on 08-01 the record was committed 51 minutes after that alert. GENERALISABLE LESSON: a delivery path where 'nothing happened' and 'nothing got through' are indistinguishable at the inbox is not a delivery path. Same shape found independently on the digest side at src/main.py:277-282, where empty-run suppression cannot distinguish 'everything deduped' from 'collection failed entirely', routing the instrument's loudest alarm exclusively through the channel that condition switches off. Fixes PROPOSED ONLY, awaiting operator sign-off.

MUTABLE-REDUCTION CITATION (integrity taxonomy entry 25) and the two relay defects that produce it. (a) scripts/fetch_relay.py's newest_request() is sorted(glob('*.json'))[-1] — LEXICOGRAPHIC on filename despite the name — and run() writes to out_dir/<request name> with no existence check. On 2026-08-05 a second batch named '2026-08-05-attribution.json' therefore re-ran the already-completed daily batch and OVERWROTE its reduction in place (run 31001060670 at 11:20:54Z replaced by run 31002416607 at 11:41:05Z), while the authorised rows went unfetched until renamed with a last-sorting prefix. The six prior batches ran correctly by coincidence of vocabulary — firing order matched lexicographic order all six times (1-in-36) — so the mechanism had never been tested, only lucky. (b) UNDERNEATH IT: twelve re-fetches of investmentpolicy.unctad.org returned TWELVE DISTINCT sha256, against a within-project negative control of every other host returning byte-identical digests across up to five runs and four hours. ESTABLISHED: an UNCTAD IIA sha256 is NOT a stable content identifier and must never be cited as a re-verifiable fingerprint, nor may two differing UNCTAD hashes be read as the page having changed. NOT ESTABLISHED and not to be asserted: the mechanism (per-request nonce vs content churn vs CDN variant) — the symptom was measured, the cause was not. CONSEQUENCE: for an UNCTAD row a re-run does not reproduce the prior reduction, it DESTROYS it. BINDING HOUSE RULE ADOPTED: every citation to a relay reduction carries the commit sha that holds it — a reduction is evidence, and a path that can be rewritten is not a citation.

OUR OWN CLIENT IS LESS COMPLIANT THAN OUR PUBLISHED METHODOLOGY CLAIMS, in two independent ways, both found with zero network access from the project's own source. (a) INTERVAL BYPASS: robots_allowed() fetches robots.txt with requests.get directly (src/sources/base.py:157), OUTSIDE _respect_rate_limit, and polite_get() calls it BEFORE _respect_rate_limit(domain) (:249 then :255). On the first fetch to any domain in a process _last_request_at has no entry, so wait == 0 and the page request follows the robots request with no enforced gap: two requests to one host back to back, every domain, every run. The 2026-08-09 relay batch did it four times. METHODOLOGY Part III publishes 'I do not send automated queries to any single domain at intervals shorter than three seconds', which is therefore FALSE AS WRITTEN. (b) WILDCARD NON-SUPPORT: Python's urllib.robotparser implements no * or $ path wildcards at all (RuleLine.applies_to is `self.path == "*" or filename.startswith(self.path)`), so this project's robots layer silently ignores every Disallow rule using a wildcard, on every host, and always has, while METHODOLOGY Part III publishes 'I follow standard robot exclusion protocols.' (b) was found by restoring the missing colon to digitallibrary.un.org's malformed 'Disallow /record/*/export/*$' line and observing that can_fetch STILL returned True — i.e. the malformed line was never load-bearing for us, and the real defect was ours. NEITHER IS PATCHED (src/ is unapproved); (a)'s fix is about two lines. Method lesson that generalises beyond these two: the day's sharpest objection was made by CONSTRUCTING the alternative worlds a check cannot distinguish and running each — three readings of a 150-character robots.txt all consistent with len(excerpt)==bytes==150, one of which inverted the day's admissibility map — which is why the reading is now recorded as CONDITIONAL rather than established.

insight: THE INSTRUMENT THIS COUNCIL USES TO CHECK ITSELF IS CONTAMINATED THREE WAYS, AND NOBODY HAD CONTROLLED IT. Every count in this record and the eight before it was produced by a git-history walk over analytics/fetch-results/ and analytics/fetch-requests/. (a) PATH-LIMITED SIMPLIFICATION: `git log <rev> -- <path>` prunes commits TREESAME to a parent across a merge, and `git rev-list <rev> -- <path>` applies the IDENTICAL simplification, so naming rev-list as the remedy licenses the same defect under another name. At origin/main scope it hid exactly three result blobs (a8a7a73f, 45ac1e3a, a2910dd6 — ranks 1, 4, 5 of 25 by fetched_at, ranks 2 and 3 retained), giving 21/19/10 where an unrestricted `git rev-list <rev>` + `ls-tree` gives 24/23/12. `git log --full-history origin/main -- analytics/fetch-results/` recovers all 24 in one command, which is the clean proof that the loss is simplification and NOT ref scope — the ref-scope diagnosis was the chairman's and it was refuted. The lost set is structurally determined and non-contiguous (whatever a merge absorbed), so it cannot be bounded by a reader from the record. (b) GRAFT PHANTOMS: this clone is SHALLOW — .git/shallow holds 10 grafts, earliest 6f1498b0 2026-07-20, latest 5bc7bd37 2026-08-04T11:19:04Z, INSIDE the record's active window — and a graft has no parents, so its whole tree reads as added and a path-limited walk reports it as touching paths it never changed: 5bc7bd37 is listed as touching scripts/fetch_relay.py while holding blob 7204847f, byte-identical to 7fbbabf's and HEAD's. Simplification UNDER-counts and grafts OVER-count, on one instrument, in one repository, on one day, composing in unknown direction. NOTHING IN THE RECORD HAD EVER SAID THIS CLONE IS SHALLOW (screened with synonyms, pinned at 26dc05b). (c) MISSING FILTER: two seats using the same command, revs and depth returned 16 blobs/15 paths and 14/14 for one directory, differing only because one filtered *.json and one did not. CONSEQUENCES ALREADY TAKEN: the chairman's 2026-08-09 tie-breaking 'fourteen commits' and the analyst's own 15-commit 'exhaustive' control are BOTH WITHDRAWN as commit counts (the latter used `git show --pretty=format: --name-only`, which prints nothing for a merge without -m/--cc, so it excluded 73 of 80 reachable merges BY CONSTRUCTION and agreed with the simplified count by coincidence); the 2026-08-08 findings are routed for re-derivation under the distinction that simplification under-counts and never invents, so an existence finding survives as a lower bound while any count, 'only', 'first' or 'never' does not. REMEDY ADOPTED (writing rules, no code): a DERIVATION PIN of four mandatory fields — COMMAND verbatim, REVS as resolved 40-char SHAs never ref names, DEPTH as shallow flag plus graft list, FILTER — plus graft commits excluded by name or the population labelled as containing them; 'local-ref scope' is RETIRED as a label because it names whatever refs the writing session happened to hold. AND THE LESSON THE PIN DOES NOT COVER: not one of the three contaminations was found by a seat checking its own work, and none would have been caught by a correctly-written pin, because each seat's pin was accurate for the derivation it ran. All three were found by two seats deriving the same figure by different means and DISAGREEING.

insight: THE PROFESSOR-FACING DIGEST ASSERTS DOCTRINAL ABSENCES ABOUT DOCUMENTS IT STATES IT NEVER READ, in 12 of 17 committed article files (plus 14 rendered index.html), 2026-06-09 through 2026-08-10. Each headline-only article file records 'Notable line: N/A - source paywalled (headline only); body not accessible' and then annotates the item with negative substantive findings about that unread body - e.g. article 03 of the 2026-08-10 digest: 'concerns vanilla mining expropriation with no intellectual property, no judicial measure, and no abuse-of-right or treaty-shopping doctrine.' That is a tool-layer status converted into a claim about the resource, four lines apart on the same page, which is the standing rule's exact prohibition - and unlike the council's own instances it is COMMITTED AND SHIPS. DIAGNOSIS (analyst's, adopted over the officer's and the chairman's): this is NOT a fabricating classifier. The annotation is a relevance screen doing its proper job - judging from a headline is the function - written in the GRAMMAR OF A FINDING ABOUT THE DOCUMENT ('contains no jurisdictional/admissibility doctrine') instead of the GRAMMAR OF A SCREEN ('nothing in the headline indicates'). So the remedy is a prompt change plus a backfill sweep, not a redesign. AGGRAVATION: one absence is demonstrably false in tendency and falls on the day's own open question - article 03 asserts 'no abuse-of-right or treaty-shopping doctrine' about a RESTRUCTURING claim against Australia, the respondent State of Philip Morris v Australia, while this council recorded the ground of that very decision today as GAP-UNRESOLVED. RULED IN-SESSION: nothing in a HEADLINE-ONLY annotation may be cited as content by any seat, retroactively across the whole digest corpus. Not patched - the classifier prompt is outside this session's approved scope.
